A systematic review was conducted to assess the relationship between household crowding and various health outcomes, supporting the development of WHO Housing and Health Guidelines. The review aimed to provide the best available evidence to inform the deliberations of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The report includes information on the population, exposure, comparator, and outcomes (PECOS), as well as eligibility criteria for the review. It also details the search strategy, methods used to identify relevant studies, and a discussion of the findings. Appendices include search strategies, evidence profiles, summary tables, and a list of excluded studies with reasons. Household crowding is defined as a situation where the number of occupants exceeds the capacity of the dwelling to provide adequate shelter, space, and privacy. It is associated with adverse health outcomes and is considered a marker of poverty and social deprivation. The review focused on priority outcomes such as close-contact infectious diseases (e.g., tuberculosis, rheumatic fever, meningococcal infections, respiratory infections), gastrointestinal diseases, psychological stress, sleep disturbances, and mental health. The review also examined the impact of crowding on children’s educational performance and other well-being outcomes. The eligibility criteria for studies included primary research with quantitative measures of crowding and its association with health outcomes. Studies were required to provide exposure-response relationships and were limited to those published from 2004 onwards. Residential housing excluded settings such as nursing homes, homeless shelters, residential schools, orphanages, hotels, and prisons. The search strategy was developed by an experienced information specialist and focused on terms related to housing and crowding. The searches were limited to studies published from 2004 onwards, with no initial restrictions on language or study design.
